THE YOUNGEST DAUGHTER

By DONALD COWIE

I HAD many remarkable experiences during my seven years' stay in the Dominion of New Zealand, but I shall not forget quickly how I came across that small desolate hut among the foothills of the Southern Alps. It is most annoying. Nor can we conceive of the beginning or end of time; for

perpetual recurrence of night and day may be

brief_context: Sent a message to the Glasgow conference as President.
brief_extract:
The Queen's Message
WHEN within three months an Association organises no less than four conferences, two national and two for area federations, at which the total attendance amounts to some seventeen hundred, it shows a phenomenal enthusiasm among the members—enthusiasm borne of conviction in the purposes of the Association. The second national conference arranged by the Electrical Association for Women this Summer was held at the Empire Exhibition, Glasgow, on the theme "The New Way of Living—Women's Work in the Modern World." To the President of the E.A.W., Her Majesty the Queen, supporter of all progressive work, graciously sent this message:
WINDSOR CASTLE
June 20th, 1938. "On the occasion of the Opening Session of your Conference at Glasgow I would ask you to convey to all the delegates my good wishes for a successful gathering.

brief_context: Author of the message sent from Windsor Castle.
brief_extract:
I recall with much pleasure my visit to your Conference at Wembley some years ago, and I am delighted to learn of the progress made in many spheres of educational work by the Association since that time. I am convinced that these efforts will prove invaluable to the young womanhood of our country to-day."
ELIZABETH R. The Queen had, at the opening of the Exhibition, visited the Association's stand in the Cultural Section of the Women of the Empire Pavilion, and seen the dioramic model "From Waterfall to Washer," which she described as "most illuminating," and upon enquiring on the progress of the work of the E.A.W., expressed satisfaction in hearing that a Domestic Workers' Certificate has been added to the other educational activities.

“THE domestic revolution might be regarded as the paying by the technicians of a long deferred debt for some of the social consequences of the mechanisation of industry last century.”
